newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan said planning new central America aid boost.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan said planning new central America aid boost.

text.p: Taiwan plans to grant an additional US$200 million in aid to its central American allies on the eve of Vice-President Lien Chan's damage-control trip to Nicaragua, a Taipei newspaper said on Sunday.
The cabinet is expected to approve the funds at a meeting on Monday, the mass circulation United Daily News quoted officials as saying.
The funds would be part of the island's economic assistance packages to boost ties with central America, it said.
Lien, who doubles as premier, is scheduled to leave on Tuesday for Nicaragua to attend the January 10 inauguration of President-elect Arnoldo Aleman.
The report did not say whether the new funds were related directly to Lien's visit.

Taipei, struggling against a diplomatic embargo imposed by longtime rival Beijing, has already agreed to offer T$1.4 billion (US$51 million) in funds to its central American allies and vowed to step up trade and investment in the region.

Wealthy but isolated Taiwan has wielded generous economic aid as a lever to help its few allies resist pressure to switch recognition to China's communist government -- a practice scorned by Beijing as "chequebook diplomacy".
Most of Taiwan's 30 diplomatic allies are underdeveloped states in central America, Africa and the Pacific.

Taiwan media have said Lien would visit Nicaragua fearing that it might be tempted to ditch Taipei in favour of Beijing after South Africa announced in November it would switch diplomatic ties to China by the end of 1997.
Pretoria had been Taiwan's biggest ally.

Taiwan and China have been rivals since a civil war ended in 1949. Beijing considers the island a renegade province and seeks to isolate Taiwan from the international arena until it can be reunified with the mainland. (US$1 = T$27.5)
